figures.description: The Driven Pile Design and Construction Process Complete design-construction process for driven pile foundations. Figure 2-3 flow chart applies to all design-bid-build projects; design-build contracts vary in early steps but the key activities remain the same. Block 1: Establish global project performance requirements (structure type, phasing, layout, site conditions) Block 2: Determine bridge geometry, substructure locations, and top of foundation elevations Block 3: Define general site geotechnical conditions, scour, and seismicity; consult hydraulic engineer for scour Block 4: Perform preliminary structural modeling to determine substructure loads and tolerable deformations Block 5: Develop and execute subsurface exploration and laboratory testing program for feasible foundation

figures.description: Pile Driving Induced Vibrations Assessment and mitigation of pile driving vibration effects on adjacent structures and soil settlement. figures.caption: Corrosion and resulting buckling of foundation pile (courtesy Wisconsin Department of Transportation)
figures.description: Durability Considerations Durability assessment and design life considerations for steel, concrete, and timber piles in various environments. AASHTO mandates 75-year design life for ordinary bridges; 100 years for complex major bridges Driven piles are generally very durable but aggressive environments can cause rapid deterioration Steel pile corrosion case: Leo Frigo Bridge (2013), Green Bay, WI - 32-year-old H-piles in porous fly ash fill with sulfates and chlorides caused 2-foot pier settlement Corrosion study of 34-year-old H-piles (Girard Avenue Bridge, Philadelphia) found 12% section loss; site-specific rate of 0.0015 in/year was less than published rates Concrete pile deterioration: chloride intrusion, reinforcement/prestressing strand corrosion, tidal/splash zone abrasion, sulfate

figures.caption: Tilting columns adjacent to stockpile (courtesy DelDOT)
figures.description: Unanticipated Occurrences Awareness of how external activities and unanticipated events can damage existing driven pile foundations. Foundation long-term performance assessed by total and differential settlement Unanticipated outside influences can compromise existing foundation performance Fill stockpile case (I-495, Delaware, 2014): ~50,000 ton stockpile near four piers caused lateral soil movement, deformed H-piles, cracked pile caps, and tilted 50-ft columns up to 2 feet Adjacent construction case (I-65, Wildcat Creek, 2015): new driven H-pile foundation released artesian pressures and sand beneath adjacent spread footing pier, causing up to 10 inches settlement and 7 inches rotation Both cases demonstrate the importance of considering effects of activities adjacent to existing pile

figures.caption: Rock core samples
figures.description: Rock Exploration Methods (Coring / Drilling) Rock exploration and quality assessment for driven pile foundations bearing on or driven to rock. Rock coring performed after soil boring encounters bedrock Conventional rotary, wire line rotary, and swelling clay/soft rock coring methods available Wire line rotary coring preferred for depths > 80 ft due to faster retrieval Rock cores stored in core boxes with notation of bedding, fractures, and weathering RQD (ASTM D6032) = sum of sound core pieces >= 4 in / total core run length RQD designations: Excellent (90-100), Good (75-90), Fair (50-75), Poor (25-50), Very Poor (<25) Core samples should be retained for project duration and beyond for construction claims RQD alone should not be used to correlate rock strength

figures.description: In-Situ Soil Testing Overview of in-situ testing methods for driven pile foundation design parameter determination. Primary in-situ tests: SPT (ASTM D1586), CPT/CPTu (ASTM D5778), VST (ASTM D2573) Lesser-used devices: PMT (ASTM D4719), DMT (ASTM D6635), dynamic cone All in-situ tests are index tests requiring local correlations In-situ tests should be benchmarked to laboratory tests where possible Each test method applies different loading conditions (orientation, rate of strain) In absence of adequate testing, engineer must use conservative approach with additional uncertainty

figures.caption: Vane shear test schematic (after Mayne et al. 2001)
figures.description: Vane Shear Test Measurement of undrained shear strength and clay sensitivity for pile design in soft to medium clays. Best suited for soft to medium clays (su < 1 ksf); not suitable in silt, sand, or gravel Four-bladed vane forced into undisturbed soil and rotated at 6 deg/min Measures both peak and remolded shear strengths for sensitivity determination Sensitivity provides qualitative indication of clay setup potential for pile drivability Rod friction must be subtracted to determine actual shear strength Can be used to depths of 13 to 20 feet without casing bore hole Quick and economical test; compares well with UC results at shallow depths
